n01.title: Central dome fresco
n01.body: Bartolomeo Altomonte painted all the ceiling pictures. The central dome fresco is the one that matters most to the library programme. Its theme is divine revelation, shown as personified divine wisdom.

n01.title: Stammel's sculptures
n01.body: Josef Stammel, the abbey's sculptor, made the sculptures in the hall in lime wood. The best known is the group "The Four Last Things": Death, Judgement, Heaven and Hell.

n01.title: The shelves
n01.body: About 60,000 volumes stand in the hall itself, out of roughly 200,000 works in the abbey collection. The most valuable items include over 1,400 manuscripts from the 8th century onwards and 530 incunabula.

n01.title: Windows
n01.body: 48 windows light the hall. Twelve more are hidden behind the bookcases.

n01.title: Down the hall
n01.body: The hall is 70 m long and 14 m wide. It is roofed by seven domes.

n01.title: Charles VI as Hercules Musarum
n01.body: The larger-than-life marble statue in the oval centre of the hall dates from 1735. It was allegedly made by the court sculptor Antonio Corradini. The other marble statues show Austrian and Spanish Habsburgs.

n01.title: Cupola fresco
n01.body: Daniel Gran painted the ceilings from 1726 to 1730. The cupola shows the apotheosis of Emperor Charles VI, with a golden medallion of the emperor held up by Apollo and Hercules.

n01.title: Venetian globe
n01.body: Four Venetian globes, each over one metre across, stand in the hall.

n01.title: Down the hall
n01.body: The hall is almost 80 m long and 20 m high. It holds around 200,000 historical books.

n01.title: Busts of poets and thinkers
n01.body: Under Duke Carl August and Goethe the library became a pantheon of Weimar Classicism. Busts of the Weimar poets and thinkers were set up, and paintings of them hung on the walls.

n01.title: Shelving by subject
n01.body: The hall now holds 40,000 volumes on the main level and first gallery. They are grouped by subject, such as history, theology and law, roughly as they stood in the mid 19th century.

n05.title: The first gallery
n05.body: The main level and the first gallery together hold 40,000 volumes. Old princely portraits were moved to the second gallery when the classical Weimar figures took their place below.

n05.title: The first gallery
n05.body: The Rokokosaal was fitted out in 1766 for Duchess Anna Amalia by Landbaumeister August Friedrich Strassburger. The main level and the first gallery together hold 40,000 volumes. About 30,000 volumes moved in during 1766.

n02.title: Main-level shelving
n02.body: The Rokokosaal holds 40,000 volumes on the main level and first gallery. The arrangement roughly follows the state of the mid-19th century and the logic of the old library's subject order.

n03.title: Busts of the Weimar writers
n03.body: Under Goethe the library became a pantheon of Weimar Classicism. The old princely portraits went to the second gallery. Busts and paintings of Weimar's poets and thinkers took their place.

n04.title: Bust of a Weimar figure
n04.body: After Goethe and Carl August died, the library became a pantheon of Weimar Classicism. Busts of the Weimar poets and thinkers were set up in the hall, and paintings of them were hung. The old princely portraits went to the second gallery.

n04.title: Shelving of the main level
n04.body: The main level and the first gallery of the Rokokosaal hold 40,000 volumes in all. The arrangement roughly follows the state of the mid-19th century.

n06.title: Balcony of the Rokokosaal
n06.body: August Friedrich Strassburger fitted out a library hall in late Rococo style inside the Green Palace, built between 1563 and 1565. The library moved in from the Residenzschloss in 1766. It held almost 30,000 volumes by then.

n06.title: Bust of a Weimar figure
n06.body: After Goethe and Carl August died, the library became a pantheon of Weimar Classicism. Busts of the Weimar poets and thinkers were set up in the hall, and paintings of them were hung. The old princely portraits went to the second gallery.

n07.title: Books under Goethe and Voigt
n07.body: In 1797 Duke Carl August put Goethe and Christian Gottlob Voigt in charge of the library. Two months after they started, they issued a new library order fixing lending days and loan periods. By 1832, the year Goethe died, the collection had reached 80,000 volumes.

n09.title: Shelves catalogued by Vulpius
n09.body: Christian August Vulpius, Goethe's brother-in-law, worked in the library from 1797 to 1826. Thanks to him, the new books were catalogued and shelved so they could be used.

x01.title: Dedication on the Washington Monument
x01.body: Lettering on the base of the monument, cut at the foot of the column. The words give the monument to George Washington in the name of the State of Maryland. The plaza the library faces is built around it.

text.original: TO GEORGE WASHINGTON / BY THE STATE OF MARYLAND
text.translation: Dedicated to George Washington by the State of Maryland.

x01.title: Washington Monument
x01.body: Robert Mills won the competition for the monument at 29. The cornerstone was laid on 4 July 1815. Enrico Causici's statue of Washington resigning his commission in 1782 was raised 178 feet up on 25 November 1829.

x01.title: Mount Vernon Place United Methodist Church
x01.body: Thomas Dixon and Charles L. Carson designed the church, completed 12 November 1872. Green serpentine from Falls Road and buff and red sandstone make six stone types. The original steeple design topped the monument, and city officials made the architect lower it.

x02.title: Washington Monument
x02.body: The column rises 178 feet 8 inches and is built of white marble from three quarries in Baltimore County. A low square base holds a gallery, and a standing figure of Washington tops the plain column. Visitors can climb 227 steps for a view of the city.

x02.title: Mount Vernon Place United Methodist Church
x02.body: The church stands on the site of Charles Howard's mansion. His father-in-law Francis Scott Key, author of The Star Spangled Banner, died there. A plaque on the south outer wall marks his death.

x03.title: Washington Monument
x03.body: The Washington Monument was the first major monument to honor George Washington. Robert Mills designed it, and construction began in 1815 on land donated by Colonel John Eager Howard. The masonry was finished by 1829.

x03.title: Mount Vernon Place United Methodist Church
x03.body: Planned as a "Cathedral of Methodism", the church cost $400,000 in 1872, including land, building and furnishings. Its colour comes from rare green serpentine metabasalt from the Falls Road area. The stone wears poorly, so repairs came in 1932 and 1978.

x04.body: The column rises 178 feet 8 inches and is built of white marble from three quarries in Baltimore County. A low square base holds a gallery, and a standing figure of Washington tops the plain column. Visitors can climb 227 steps for a view of the city.

x05.body: The church stands on the site of Charles Howard's mansion. His father-in-law Francis Scott Key, author of The Star Spangled Banner, died there. A plaque on the south outer wall marks his death.

x01.title: The Ciudadela building
x01.body: This red stone building was the Royal Tobacco Factory of New Spain, finished in 1807. José María Morelos was held here in 1815. In 1944 the property was given over to a library, which opened on 27 November 1946 with José Vasconcelos as first director.

r01.title: The apse
r01.body: A large arched niche closes the far wall, above a crypt that held the donor's sarcophagus. Strocka writes: "We will never know whose statue stood in the apse of the Celsus library." The image leaves the niche empty, in the centre of the far wall.

r01.title: Niches beside the apse
r01.body: Strocka records two niches on each side of the apse. The image shows niches with wooden doors beside the apse, on two levels. The doors and frames are guesses.

r01.title: Wall niches for cupboards
r01.body: Ten niches were left in the walls of the 16.72 by 10.92 m hall at floor level: two on each side of the apse and three each on the south and north walls. Each is 2.55 m high and 0.57 to 0.60 m deep. Strocka reconstructs thirty wall cabinets in three rows and calls the third row probable. The image shows tall niches on the long walls, some with wooden doors, in two rows, and three per wall cannot be counted in it. The doors and the stone frames are guesses.

r01.title: The podium
r01.body: In front of the niches ran a continuous podium 0.94 m high and 1.02 m wide, with no steps up to it. Attendants would have used movable wooden steps. The image shows a continuous marble podium with no steps along the walls. Its height and width are not checked against the metres.

r01.title: Columns on the podium
r01.body: Traces in the back wall show that columns stood on the podium. The image has fluted Corinthian marble columns standing on it. The capital style and the marble colour are guesses.

r01.title: Gallery level
r01.body: Traces in the back wall show that columns carried an entablature and a gallery floor about 4.30 m above the podium, and Strocka thinks a second, shorter row of columns carried a third level. The image shows a gallery level with a shorter row of columns above it. The balustrade and the openings behind the columns are guesses.

r01.title: Entrance wall
r01.body: Strocka records three entrances in the facade wall, the middle one wider and higher, with windows above them. The entrance wall is split across the two edges of the image and shows a single doorway with an opening above it and daylight beyond. One doorway is wrong: the record has three.

r01.title: Ceiling
r01.body: Strocka gives the wooden ceiling as 12.15 m above the marble floor. The image has a plain flat timber ceiling, which fits the record. The record says nothing about how the ceiling was finished, so the plank pattern is a guess.

r01.title: Marble floor
r01.body: Strocka records a marble floor. The image has one. The slab layout is a guess.

r01.title: Book racks on the foundation
r01.body: Bohn found a foundation 1.05 m wide along the three standing walls of a room 16.95 m deep and 13.53 m wide, set about 0.50 m in from them, with dowel holes, and read it as the footing for wooden book racks. He says the height of the racks cannot be given. The image puts open wooden racks on a stone strip, but the strip runs against the wall instead of 0.5 m in from it. The five rows and the form of the racks are guesses.

r01.title: Shelves, left empty
r01.body: The sources read give no find of books in this room, so the shelves are shown empty. The shelf pattern is a guess.

r01.title: Wall finish
r01.body: The image shows plaster with a painted band under the ceiling over a marble plinth. Bohn's finds in this room are the foundation, the dowel holes and the stone plates. The sources read record no wall finish, so the plaster, the plinth, the band and the colours are guesses.

r01.title: Where Bohn put Athena
r01.body: Bohn found a projection 2.74 m wide and 1.05 m out in the middle of the north side, and a statue base 1.19 m was found in the rubble of the stoa. The image has a plain block standing free in front of the far wall and no statue. A free block is not a projection of the wall, so it does not match.

r01.title: Timber ceiling
r01.body: Exposed curved beams and boards. The roof and ceiling of the room are not known from the sources read, so this is a guess.

r01.title: Connecting doorway
r01.body: Layard describes two small chambers that opened into each other. The doorway to a second chamber stands for that link. Its size and frame are guesses.

r01.title: Fish-cloaked figures
r01.body: Layard says the first doorway was guarded by fish-gods. The image puts a relief figure in a fish cloak on each side of the doorway. How they were carved, their height and their pose are guesses.

r01.title: Ruined wall slabs
r01.body: Layard found the bas-reliefs of these chambers mostly destroyed. The image shows cracked, blackened slabs with almost no carving left. The pattern of the damage is a guess.

r01.title: Broken tablets on the floor
r01.body: Layard found the chambers filled a foot or more deep with clay tablets, most of them broken. The largest were about 9 by 6.5 inches and the smallest about an inch long. The image covers the floor with broken pieces. The pieces nearest the viewer are larger than those sizes, and the marks on them are not real cuneiform.

r01.title: Roof beams
r01.body: Sennacherib's inscriptions say the palace halls were roofed with beams of cedar and cypress. That is borrowed here: the roof of this small chamber is not known. The image shows straight timber beams under reed matting. The matting is a guess, and the beams look slightly curved because of the image projection.

r01.title: Shelves around the walls
r01.body: Wikipedia, citing Amedeo Maiuri, says the rolls lay in wooden capsae, some of them on shelves around the walls. It counts over 1,800 rolls. The image has open wooden shelves with cupboards below, holding stacks of rolls. The shelf heights, the panelled cupboard doors and their knobs are guesses.

r01.title: Double-sided shelf unit
r01.body: Maiuri, as Wikipedia reports him, puts some rolls on the two sides of a set of shelves in the middle of the room. The image has a free-standing unit with rolls on two sides. Its size and shape are guesses.

r01.title: Charred rolls
r01.body: The Getty gives approximately 1,100 carbonized rolls recovered between 1752 and 1754, many of them writings of Philodemus of Gadara. The image shows mostly dark, charred rolls here, which fits the find. Whether the room held them in this stacked form is not known.

r01.title: Pale rolls, a mismatch
r01.body: Some rolls on the left and rear shelves are pale tan, as intact papyrus would be. The real rolls were charred black by the eruption of AD 79. These do not match the record.

r01.title: Plain plaster
r01.body: Plain cream plaster walls, a red marble skirting and a smooth vaulted ceiling. No wall finish from this room appears in the sources read, so all of it is a guess.

r01.title: Mosaic floor
r01.body: The Getty shows an in-situ mosaic floor with a meander in room O of the Villa, first century BC. It does not say which room held the rolls. A floor of this kind is borrowed here from elsewhere in the building. The pattern drawn is a guess.

r01.title: The public walk
r01.body: Strabo writes that the Museum is part of the palaces and has a public walk. The curved colonnade stands for that walk. The column style, the curve, the roof and the proportions are guesses.

r01.title: Place with seats
r01.body: Strabo also lists a place furnished with seats. He gives no size or look. The curved stone steps are invented and look more like a small theatre than anything he describes.

r01.title: Door to the large hall
r01.body: Strabo names a large hall in which the men of learning of the Museum take their common meal. He does not say where it stood or what it looked like. The stone block and its doorway are a guess.

r01.title: Sea and gardens
r01.body: Sea, palms, cypresses and distant pedimented buildings beyond the walk. Strabo's sentence gives no view. They are invented.

r01.title: Paving
r01.body: Stone slabs. Nothing is recorded of the surface. A tower-shaped shadow falls across them to one side, and no building in the image casts it.

r01.title: Mural of two trees
r01.body: The Dunhuang Academy records a Late Tang painting of two trees on the north wall of Cave 17. Under one tree stands an attendant with staffs and a towel, under the other a nun with a fan, with a cloth bag and a water vessel hung from the branches. The image shows both figures, the bags and the trees. A third tree and a figure appear at the left edge of the image. They are not in the record.

r01.title: Low platform on the north wall
r01.body: A low rectangular platform of meditation-bed type fills the foot of the north wall. A seated stucco statue of the monk Hongbian stood on it, since the cave began as his memorial chamber. The image shows a seated monk on a plain platform. The statue was moved elsewhere when the cave was used to store manuscripts, so the face, robe and pose are guesses.

r01.title: The manuscript heap
r01.body: Aurel Stein described bundles heaped in layers, a solid mass nearly ten feet high that left floor room for about two people. Around 50,000 documents are estimated, among them about 1,100 bundles of scrolls. The image has neat stacks about waist to shoulder high against one wall and plenty of open floor. That is tidier and far emptier than Stein's account. How the bundles were wrapped when the cave was closed is not known.

r01.title: The doorway
r01.body: Cave 17 faces south and has no antechamber or corridor of its own. It opens off the north wall of the corridor of Cave 16 and was walled up in the early eleventh century. The image has a framed door on the wall beside the platform wall, where the record puts the opening opposite the platform, on the south. A long corridor runs beyond the door. Both the door position and the corridor are wrong.

r01.title: Flat ceiling, a mismatch
r01.body: The Academy record gives the cave a truncated-pyramid ceiling (覆斗形顶) with no murals. The image has a flat, rough, unpainted ceiling. The bare surface agrees with the record. The flat shape does not.

r01.title: Bare plaster walls
r01.body: The east and south walls of Cave 17 carry no murals. The image has bare rough plaster there. The plaster colour, the roughness and the warm light are guesses; nothing in the record says how the cave looked inside when it was sealed.

r01.title: Stele of 851
r01.body: The Academy record lists a stele of 851 set into the west wall, carrying the text of the imperial edict honouring Hongbian. The image shows a carved stone stele on a base, standing free beside the door. The characters on it are not real writing and are not the edict.

r01.title: Gilded shelves
r01.body: Naldo Naldi describes gilded shelves in three rows running all around the walls, with the books grouped by content. The image has wooden shelves with gilt trim round the walls, but they appear to have four rows, not three. The books stand upright with their spines out. The sources do not say how the books were placed.

r01.title: Curtains against dust
r01.body: Curtains woven of coloured and gold thread protected the books from dust. The image has swagged brocade curtains in blue, red and gold, tied back at each bay. How they hung and their exact colours are guesses.

r01.title: Two stained-glass windows
r01.body: The room had two stained-glass windows with the king's couch between them. The image has two tall pointed windows with coloured heraldic glass. The window style, the arched shape and the pattern of the glass are guesses.

r01.title: The king's couch
r01.body: The king's couch stood between the windows under a golden cloth. The image has a carved couch under a gold cloth below the windows. The cloth is the attested part; the shape of the couch is a guess.

r01.title: Carved chests
r01.body: Books too numerous for the shelves lay in richly carved chests beneath them. The image has carved wooden chests under each shelf bay. The carving pattern and the way they join the shelf bases are guesses.

r01.title: Chairs
r01.body: Csapodi, following Naldi, lists three-legged chairs for readers. The image has three-legged stools with cushioned tops and no backs. They are stools, not chairs, and the design is a guess.

r01.title: Bindings
r01.body: Corvinus codices were bound in gilded leather or in red, green, blue or violet silk or velvet, with the king's arms, gilded silver studs and enamelled clasps. The image shows red, blue and gold bindings standing upright, with gilt shields of arms across groups of spines. The colours loosely agree with the record. No source says arms showed on the spines, and the spine layout and clasps are not taken from any surviving codex.

r01.title: The vault
r01.body: Csapodi's account gives a vault painted with the constellation of the stars at the moment Matthias became king of Bohemia in 1469. The image has a deep blue vault with gold stars and constellation figures, which follows that account. The star pattern is not the real 1469 sky. Csapodi reports that an adjoining room was added later, and Miklos Olah describes two connected vaulted rooms. The image shows one.

r01.title: Floor
r01.body: No source read describes the floor, the room dimensions or the vault height. The stone flag floor, the ribbed vault, the candle sconces, the side tables and the proportions of the room are invented.

r01.title: Row of monks' cells
r01.body: Every excavated monastery at Nalanda is a rectangle with a central court, a verandah and an outer row of cells for the monks. The image shows two storeys of open cells with small niches round the court. The count, size and doorways are not tied to one monastery.

r01.title: The pillared verandah
r01.body: Excavators found a pillared verandah around the court of several monasteries. Only the brick footing and plan survive. The image draws it as brick pillars on both storeys. The material, spacing and height are guesses; the timber posts and beams are not shown.

r01.title: The court well
r01.body: The sources give a well in the monastery court, with drains carrying water out. The image has a round brick well with drains running across the paving. The round shape, the curb, its size and the drain layout are the image's guess.

r01.title: Shrine opposite the entrance
r01.body: Several monasteries have a central shrine chamber facing the entrance across the court. Monastery 1 held a colossal seated Buddha. The image has a seated Buddha in a deep niche. The niche, the figure and its size are invented.

r01.title: Stairs to an upper floor
r01.body: The excavated monasteries have staircases in the south-west corner. The image has a straight brick stair on the right side of the court. That position is not sourced. Xuanzang also mentions towers and upper rooms rising above the clouds, which excavations do not confirm in detail.

r01.title: No roof shown
r01.body: The image leaves the walls open to the sky, with no roof at all. Nothing excavated tells us how Nalanda's monasteries were roofed, so this is a gap, not a finding. The library is not in this view: the three Dharmaganja buildings known from Tibetan tradition have not been found.

r01.title: Vents in the back wall
r01.body: The Archaeological Survey of India reports a rectangular library building with a range of vents in its back wall, letting in air cooled by water from the reservoir next to it. The image has square vents low on the wall facing the water and repeats them on another face of the block. The record gives them in the back wall only. Their shape, size and number and the wall height are guesses.

r01.title: The adjoining reservoir
r01.body: The reservoir beside the library is part of the excavated record, and the vents are tied to it. The image has a long rectangular pool with a brick curb. Its shape, banks and water level are invented.

r01.title: Narrow corridor to the monastery
r01.body: The library stands about 32 m south of the monastery, at its south-west corner, joined to it by a narrow corridor. The image has a long walled brick path running from the reservoir toward the monastery, and it meets the outer wall with no visible doorway into it. Its width, walls and paving are guesses.

r01.title: The monastery and stupa
r01.body: The excavated monastery is a square 330 m on each side with 208 cells, 52 a side, round a cruciform stupa about 15 m high. The image has a low walled square with a stepped pyramid in the middle. The stupa is not cruciform and the pyramid is wrong. The same square vents are repeated along the monastery wall, which the record does not give, and the cells are not visible.

r01.title: Brick fabric
r01.body: The wall material of the library is not given in the sources read. Brick is taken from the rest of the site, whose terracotta plaques and brickwork are well documented. The image has plain brick coursing on a very tall block with no openings above the vents. The courses and colour are borrowed, not recorded, and the height is more than any source supports.

r01.title: Trees, low wall and haze
r01.body: The trees on the horizon, the flat plain and the clear sky are invented. No source read describes the surroundings.

r01.title: Thatched main hall
r01.body: The city's plan gives the Hojo of the restored area a thatched hip-and-gable roof. The large hall in the image has a thatched roof and wooden walls. It is a building of that kind, not a portrait of the real Hojo.

r01.title: Board-roofed outbuildings
r01.body: The city's plan lists board roofs for the Shoin, Shuryo and the new storehouse, and lists the Kuri under both thatch and board. The long low buildings at the left and right of the image have board roofs and no tiles, which agrees. Which of them is which building is not known.

r01.title: Rocks and planting
r01.body: The north and south gardens were restored to match picture maps, according to the city's plan. The image has a rock-edged planting bed with clipped shrubs and no pond. The layout and the rocks were not taken from those maps and are invented.

r01.title: Pines and planting
r01.body: The city plan names a historic pine (Jifuri-matsu) among the site's features but gives no planting layout. The single shaped pine in this view is invented and is not that tree.

r01.title: Bamboo fence
r01.body: The bamboo fence, the plain gravel yard, the thatched gate on the right and the wooded hills behind are guesses. No source read describes the enclosure or its materials.

r01.title: What is not in view
r01.body: The Confucius temple hall (Daiseiden) and the School Gate stand in the west zone and are historic buildings, not rebuilt. They are not in this image. The restored buildings stand in the east. Where the books were kept in the Edo period is not covered by sources read here.

x04.title: Jardin Vivienne
x04.body: A 1,900 m2 garden on rue Vivienne at the Richelieu site, by Mirabelle Croizier, Antoine Quenardel and Gilles Clement. Its plants are those used for writing materials: paper mulberry, bamboo, rice-paper plant, papyrus and paper birch. It reinstates the garden of Mazarin's palace, later recreated by Labrouste.

x01.title: Bibliotheque Nationale doorway
x01.body: The words BIBLIOTHEQUE NATIONALE are carved above this doorway on rue Vivienne. This is the Richelieu site of the BnF. The library says the site has two entrances, at 58 rue de Richelieu and 5 rue Vivienne, and is open to all, with a cafe, a book shop and a garden.

x02.title: Gate and trees on rue Vivienne
x02.body: An iron gate with trees behind it, beside the library front on rue Vivienne. The BnF describes a 1,900 m2 garden on rue Vivienne at this site, on the ground where Cardinal Mazarin had the garden of his palace laid out in the 17th century.

x03.title: Richelieu's southern corner
x03.body: The Richelieu block from near rue Vivienne and rue des Petits-Champs. The BnF's own history bounds the site by these two streets, along with rue de Richelieu and rue Colbert. It also places Galerie Colbert on the other side of rue Vivienne.

x05.title: Richelieu's north-east corner
x05.body: The Richelieu block near rue Vivienne and rue Colbert. The BnF says the last north-east plots at this corner were acquired in 1882, allowing Jean-Desire Pascal to complete the quadrilateral with new buildings, including the Salle Ovale.
